utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Judge Fluegge is, for urgent personal reasons, unable to continue sitting in this case, this part-heard case, for a short period - that is, for today - and Judge Moloto and myself have considered whether it would be in the interests of justice to continue to hear the case today and we decided that it was. Therefore, we'll sit 15 bis today. Yesterday it was announced that there was a short preliminary matter, although not to be dealt with in 30 seconds, to be dealt with before Mr. Milutinovic would start his -- giving his testimony. Who may I address? Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. To address this matter, if we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules require that you make a solemn declaration before you give evidence. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Milutinovic. Mr. Milutinovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is counsel -- is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I wish you a good day.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecutors, General Mladic, good morning to you all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Milovan Milutinovic, my father's name was Mico.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can call up in e-court 1D1743.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, there is a signature on the first page of this statement. Can you tell us whose signature appears on this first page?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can now turn to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is visible on this last page of the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Again, mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, subsequent to signing this statement, did you have occasion to read the same to check if everything is correctly written in it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I read it a few times. I believe it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If asked questions on the same topics as contained in your statement today, would your answers be the same today as contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I would probably provide a much longer statement. However, I was directed by the lawyers to make my statement as short and as concise as possible, but I wouldn't change anything in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have taken a declaration to tell the truth today. Does that mean that the answers as recorded in your statement are truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely in keeping with the solemn declaration that I just gave, everything I stated is truthful and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender 1D1743 into evidence. There are no associated exhibits with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01743 receives Exhibit Number D862, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D862 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a public summary to read of the witness statement, the topic of the same, which has been advised to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From 1992 to 1994, Colonel Milovan Milutinovic was chief of the press centre and chief of information service at the command of the 5th JNA Corps which became the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS. From 1994 to 1996, he was the head of information service and centre for information and propaganda activities of the Main Staff of the VRS. The witness hails from the village of Trnopolje, near Prijedor. He notes that during World War II the Ustasha murdered 700.000 Serbs, Jews, and Roma in Jasenovac, and that 450 Serbs of Kozarac were murdered by their Muslim and Croat neighbours at that time, including the witness's grandfather and ten relatives. The witness recalled that Sarajevo and the other declared safe zones were supposed to be demilitarised but that UNPROFOR commander Briquemont confirmed the Muslims are using the zones protected by the UN to mount attacks on the Serb positions from there. The witness recalled that Muslim forces in Sarajevo breached the cease-fire agreement on 21 May 1995 by attacking Serb positions from the safe area of Sarajevo. On this occasion, the Muslim forces were supported by artillery fire from the Egyptian Battalion of UNPROFOR. He held an international press conference of the Main Staff where the violation of the cease-fire and the abuse of authority by the Egyptian Battalion were protested against by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness further recalled that in relation to Markale 2, that Russian investigative teams involved in the UNPROFOR joint commission established that some victims of Markale 2 were individuals who had perished earlier and whose bodies had been exchanged prior to Markale 2. Per the witness, research shows the Muslim authorities sacrificed their own compatriots in a bread-line massacre in 1992 in addition to both Markale incidents and opened fire on their own people, journalists, and UNPROFOR to blame the Serbs. The witness recalled that at the BiH Assembly Alija Izetbegovic stated: "For a sovereign BiH, I am even willing to sacrifice peace." Alija Izetbegovic withdrew his signature on the already concluded Cutileiro Peace Agreement on the advice of American Ambassador Zimmerman. Since the beginning of 1991, the Muslim leadership was preparing in an organised manner for an armed conflict. In a magazine interview with Izetbegovic from 1994, Izetbegovic said that the Patriotic League was established on 10 June 1991 to prepare the people for defence and arm them. The Patriotic League had nine regional and 103 municipal staff with 98.000 armed combatants, according to General Sefer Halilovic. The arrival of Mujahedin to Bosnia ensued after the Grand Mufti and Alija Izetbegovic issued a fatwa on jihad. As to Srebrenica, the witness recalls that General Mladic received a delegation of Muslims that that expressed their wish to leave. Mladic told them. "... I give my word of a general that all those who gather around the check-point in Potocari can choose whether to go to Yugoslavia, to the Federation, or to stay in Republika Srpska ... I guarantee you full freedoms and rights ..." When the talks with the Muslims were finished, he told General Krstic: "... behave like knights. I gave my word of a general. No one must be harmed ..." The witness remembers being on Boksanica hill in July 1995 near Zepa with General Mladic when General Rupert Smith, in the presence of UNHCR, OSCE, and US officials --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- commended General Mladic for the treatment of the Srebrenica population by the VRS, and asked for fair treatment of the Zepa population which General Mladic promised. The witness is of the opinion that as an officer and a man General Mladic could never issue an order that would be in contravention of the Geneva Conventions. The witness is deeply sorry about all the victims, and believes the real perpetrators should answer for these crimes. And that ends the summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any further questions for the witness, please put them to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to look at paragraph 14 [sic] to be found on page 25 in both versions of your statement. Sir, this attack by the ABiH which violated the cease-fire and when the Egyptian Battalion participated in the same, what response, if any, was there by UNPROFOR after your press conference and General Mladic's protests?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you dealing with paragraph 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 114, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 114? That's correct. After the ABH army attacked from Sarajevo with the artillery support from the UNPROFOR contingent, together with General Mladic, we organised a press conference at Pale. I condemned the unilateral violation of the cease-fire by the Muslim forces. My position at that press conference was that the United Nations thus sided up with just one -- with just one side during the conflict in Bosnia. To answer your question: As far as I know, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the best words spoken until now, "to answer your question," because you're supposed to do nothing else than to answer the question. It was not whether you gave a press conference. That was all the included in the question. What was the response, if any, by UNPROFOR to that press conference and the protests.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] UNPROFOR didn't react at all. The Serbian forces in Jahorinski Potok were bombarded by NATO in retaliation against the Army of Republika Srpska. In other words, there was no objective answer from that side. No response at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 44, found on page 12 in the English, page 11 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph you talk of Penny Marshall filming from within a fenced-in warehouse, filming the people at Trnopolje who were outside the fenced-in area. Did you ever talk to Ms. Marshall about why she was filming in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I received an order concerning a group of foreign journalists who had arrived from London. There were some 30 of them. I was to take them to Prijedor, Trnopolje, and Omarska. I was against that because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again, please start by answering the question. Did Penny Marshall, did you ever talk to her about why she was filming in this way? So we would like to hear about any conversation you may have had with Penny Marshall on this subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I need to explain. I took 30 journalists first to the staff for the talks there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, to some extent that's already in your statement. And apart from that, it's the question and it's Mr. Ivetic who defines what we would like to hear from you. Did you have any conversation with Penny Marshall on this subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For her own security she entered the compound that had a wire fence around it and started recording. When I mentioned that, when I warned her about it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She went in to protect herself from extremists. And when I asked her why she did that, she said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat that last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She told me that because of her own personal security, safety, she entered the construction material depot and started recording because she was afraid of the reaction of the people around her. But when I warned her that she had abused our hospitality, she said that that footage that was recorded would not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to page 26 in the English and it's at the bottom of page 25, on the top of page 26 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And paragraph 118 of your statement. Sir, here I want to ask you: How did you come to learn of these conclusions by the Russian members of the UNPROFOR joint commission that these -- that the Markale victims consisted of bodies killed prior and exchanged prior?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska received information from the investigative commission, Russian component, who was investigating what happened in Markale II. And in that report it said that some previously killed persons were found among the bodies who had been probably exchanged a few days before between the Muslim and Serbian side. So the information service made an announcement of the Main Staff and in the information we mentioned the data we received from the Russian members of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what reaction, if any, did you note from General Smith or UNPROFOR following this information?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: There was no reaction. Quite the opposite. A couple of days later Republika Srpska -- actually, the 15-day bombing started of the whole territory of Republika Srpska by the NATO airforce.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a few follow-up questions in relation to this. Was it verified, were those persons identified who had been exchanged? Was the identity known of those persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I personally don't know that. We just received the information from the Russian delegation which was part of the investigation team, so I cannot really give you an affirmative answer to that because there was no time to check this, either. My information service was not obliged to check or verify this. The documents we received from them were part of the Main Staff archives, and they went together with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was -- were the identities of those persons verified later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said "probably they were exchanged." So do I understand that that's just a probability and not for a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that we received from the Russian part of the commission said that. I don't know anything different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That document you are talking about we -- this witness often refers to documents of which I'm not always certain whether we have them or not. Does it ring any bell as to what exhibit we should look at or is any of the parties inclined or intending to provide such documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can say that I was planning on searching through it. I, from off the top of my head, had not recalled a single document of this nature, which is why I have asked the witness to give further details because I was -- when I read the statement I did not recall a document of that nature. But I will, of course, endeavour to find it if it exists because I think it would be very helpful for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you know, we have no documents from this report, and I'm not aware of any Russian -- such Russian documents. We'll, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- look for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, this Chamber, if you could assist us in finding the document, then of course the Chamber would -- would be happy to receive any document which is not known to it until now. So if you would have it or know where it is, don't hesitate to tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are documents that were in the Main Staff archives. The bulk of the archives were taken by UNPROFOR in the presence of President Biljana Plavsic from the base in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you could clarify for us, was it UNPROFOR or IFOR that took those documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: IFOR. In 1996. It was IFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to look at page 8 in the English, page 7 in the Serbian, and paragraph 24 of your statement. Here you talk of the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia. Are you aware if General Mladic or the Main Staff ever advised UNPROFOR of the presence of these Croatian troops in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I myself believe that the Main Staff of Republika Srpska sent protests more than ten times to the UNPROFOR command and to the United Nations regarding the presence of some 10- to 15.000 regular Croatian army forces, which constituted an aggression on the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In that regard, we had the United Nations Secretary General send a strong protest requesting Croatia to withdraw their forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina. In response to that, Croatia said that there was an agreement between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia from June 1991, and that is what they used to justify the presence of their forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Somewhat later in 1995 General Mladic and I held a press conference in Banja Luka where we mentioned all the Croatian army brigades that took part in the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can move to paragraph 50 of your statement, found on page 12 in the Serbian, page 13 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are those protests, written protests, are they - and I'm looking at the parties - are they somewhere in evidence or are they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know -- do you know where they are, these protests? Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these documents are contained in the Main Staff archives, documents sent to UNPROFOR and the United Nations. I am sure that that exists, but they just need to be admitted into the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can check on that. I do recall at least one of -- one such document that I used with General Smith which I believe is the letter from General Janvier from General Mladic, but I can -- I can get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be. But, Witness, as you may understand, this Chamber, whenever you refer to any documents or any information we'd like to know exactly what documents do exist and where that information is to be found and where it comes from. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe we were going to paragraph 50, found on page 12. If we're there. Sir, in this paragraph you say the international public was silent about the Mujahedin presence until the arrived of the Americans as part of IFOR. What happened and what changed with the arrival of the Americans in regard to the Mujahedin in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The US administration and the entire European public was permanently aware of the arrival of the Mujahedin to Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is confirmed by a study of the offensives on the Balkans where he says that there were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you again slow down. The interpreters are unable to follow your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] US journalists began to write about the Mujahedin more objectively and in more detail only after the end of the war when the decision was made for the IFOR forces to arrive to implement peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina whereby the key role was played by US troops. In that regard, Joseph Bosanski, director of the Centre for Strategic Research wrote about the Balkans and the presence of 12- to 18.000 Mujahedin in Bosnia-Herzegovina and how they posed a latent danger for all international forces that would be found in order to implement the peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is well known that Islamic forces arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the request of Alija Izetbegovic and Reis Ceric, who in 1992 proclaimed jihad, meaning a call to all Muslims of the world to join the fight against the infidel Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you say 8- to 12.000. I just heard you say 12- to 18.000. Which of the two is the correct reflection of what was written by Mr. Bosanski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the interpretation was incorrect: 8- to 12.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. My last question deals with paragraph 30 of your statement found on page 9 in both versions. Sir, in this paragraph you identify journalists working at the press centre that were Croat or Muslim in ethnicity and that remained throughout the war. Were these journalists members of any army, and if so, which army were they members of?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this question. The press centre of the corps and the Main Staff also had journalists who were Croats and Muslims. I just briefly mentioned that in the statement. I mentioned two of them. They were members of the Army of Republika Srpska. I have to say that other than that, the 1st Krajina Corps also had a Muslim battalion called Mesa Selimovic from Derventa that comprised an all Muslim personnel including the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, on behalf of the General Mladic and the rest of my team I thank you for answering my questions this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Milutinovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. You'll find Mr. McCloskey to your right. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It appeared to me that you understand some English; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: None at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your position at the Main Staff's centre for information and propaganda, did you consider yourself a professional propagandist?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I must say -- may I answer? Is this a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a question. You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our earlier composition of the Yugoslav People's Army, by establishment there was a section that was dealing with propaganda and information. But the propaganda was not conceived in the way certain circles are implementing that; for example, the Armed Forces of the United States and the French. In their case these are psych-ops. Propaganda in the classical sense is not propaganda but just dealing with facts with the objective of persuading appropriate circles about the need to implement specific solutions or to accept existing positions. So in that sense the propaganda was directed primarily towards one's own citizens and population in order to inform them and to prepare them in order to carry out the suitable mobilisation in order to be able to wage a defensive war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that definition of propaganda. That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you ask whether the witness considers himself to be a propagandist, then of course there should be clarity about what propaganda and what a propagandist is. So in that respect, I must --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was my next question as I agree with you. But before I get there, I would like to know if he does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- so that his answer will have more meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you consider yourself -- did you at that time consider yourself a propagandist?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I completed senior JNA political school for political information and morale, and I am responsible in my opinion for that area. I also carried out some propaganda tasks, but I believe that I was not a propagandist per se in that sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you disseminate VRS propaganda to your own people?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: This was in my job description and part of the remit of the press centre for information and propaganda services of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you did disseminate VRS propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, meaning that it involved truthful information, presentation of appropriate positions, and informing the population about the need to mobilise assets and means in order to be able to carry out a defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's your position that the VRS propaganda was truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part it was truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the Muslim propaganda truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Croat propaganda --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: That is how we understood propaganda. That of the Croats as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did the international forces use propaganda in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you felt that was truthful as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. I just have to differentiate here. In our language I have to make a difference between "propaganda" and "manipulation," as well as psychological activities that at a certain point were waged against the Serbian people by certain Western circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who wrote your statement, Defence 862?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The statement that we were reading out now, is that the one you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The attorneys worked on it together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the attorneys actually typed it up?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I mean those -- Lukic and his colleague, the two people who are mentioned in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who provided the information that went into what they were typing?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I did. Who else could it have been? They were interviewing me. And then when they drafted the final document, they gave it to me to see whether I agreed with it and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you check the sources you make? You make many media and other sources. Did you check those sources to make sure they're accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I did check all the sources. For the most part they are correct. I published four studies about the war in Bosnia, and I think here you have all four of my published books and they also refer to appropriate sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the most part they're correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that suggests part of it's not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: There are some sources in the statement about which in the meantime I did not provide verification material. I don't have for them sources where this information comes from, but I do have that information and there are documents to substantiate those items.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you've just said you've got information in the report that you have provided no verification material. All right. I'll go on. Let's go to your report, D862, page 24 in the English. It also should be page 24 in the B/C/S. Looking at the paragraphs 109. You're talking about situations here where you're saying the Muslims killed or terrorised their own people. And on paragraph 110, you say: "There are numerous other testimonies by Western reporters about the Muslim forces abusing their fellow citizens in order to accuse the Serbs and ensure the engagement of NATO in support of the Muslim forces. Thus, the British journalist Martin Bell wrote in the 'Sunday': 'I felt like a poor foot soldier in the army whose entire Muslim command lost their mind and terrorised their own people - and I told them that,' wrote Martin Bell on 3 July 1994 in the 'Independent Sunday' about the media manipulation after his stay in the BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I want to go to 65 ter 31811.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We did go to the 3rd July 1994 "Sunday Independent" that you cite in your statement, and we did find a quote from Martin Bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we translated part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that you can read it. But I will read some of this out loud. We see that it's under the heading in this lengthy article called: "Real-time reporting can have direct short-term effect on events. Here are examples." Then we'll go down to the part we translated for you, and it gives an example of the controversial British air-lift after the BBC report about Irma Hadzimuratovic on a light weekend news day last August showed the power and resentment television crews can make. "Irma's story struck an emotional cord with viewers in a way less personalised coverage could not have done. The media clamour for action saved Irma and resulted in offers of 1800 hospital beds worldwide, which the aid agencies could not otherwise have secured."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not found it yet in the English version, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be page 4 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just above the middle of the page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then starting with the paragraph that says: "But the process created a bitter, destabilising inter-agency confrontation over the priorities in evacuation procedures for the injured. Some found it hard to comprehend the actions of the news organisations and the British government," quote, from Martin Bell, "'I felt like a humble foot soldier in an army whose high command had taken leave of its collective senses - and I told them so,' said Martin Bell." Now, to remind us what you said in support of your theory that the Muslims were killing themselves, quote from your report: "I felt like a poor foot soldier in the army whose entire Muslim command lost their mind and terrorised their own people - and I told them that." Now, your quote adds "Muslim command" and "terrorised their own people." And we can see from Mr. Bell's quote he is talking about an issue he has with his own government and how they reacted to this situation. How on earth, sir, did you do this to Martin Bell's quote?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't speak English, I don't read English. I used a Tanjug report. Perhaps I should have added who my source was because I used the Tanjug report, and I am talking about the Belgrade-based news agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask you the following: Is it true that whatever reference, direct reference to English texts or English publications, that you have not verified them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not verify them because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I thought the Tanjug was a trustworthy agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. We'll take a break, Witness, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, on paragraph 85 of your statement you say that you give an interview with the Netherlands Institute on War Documentation, known as NIOD, who we've heard a little bit about in this courtroom, and I would like to take you to their report of your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is at 65 ter 31807. It should be page 13 in the English and page 13 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on paragraph -- what they note as their paragraph 53 of their notes or their statements on your interview, they say that you -- you provided information, and I quote, that: "During a military operation, Milutinovic and his assistants were not allowed in the operations area." Is that correct, that during military operations you and your assistants were not allowed in the operations area?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: This is wrong, wrongly interpreted. This conversation was of a private nature, and I sent a protest letter asking why a document of that kind was ever submitted to the Tribunal, since it was a free-flowing conversation between two historians who wanted to take a closer look at the situation. During the military operation not just me but journalists, teams of journalists were not allowed to enter the zone of Srebrenica. Why am I saying this? Because I, my journalist, and my photographer, came to Srebrenica to talk to the Dutch Battalion, and on the following day I was to attend --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir -- sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: -- the talks between General Mladic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we may get into that narrative but I think you've answered my question in some way. Let me ask you another part of it. It also goes on to say: "They were never informed in advance of planned operation," meaning you and your team were never performed -- or, excuse me, you were never informed in advance of planned operations. Is that true? Was that the way it was, that the -- the press information and propaganda people weren't given prior notice of operations?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: This proves that in the military there was a mismatch between the real needs and -- what was needed and what existed in the field. Although we were an integral part of the Army of Republika Srpska, journalists were considered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you can insist on an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, it was a simple question: Were you and your people not -- were never informed in advance of planned operations?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Not always but occasionally, yes. For -- we were not informed about certain operations because they were carried out at the tactical and operational level. But we were informed about larger-scale operations. I read NIOD's report. There are a lot of misinterpretations. I've not seen this document before, mind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You haven't seen your report of your interview from NIOD, is what you mean? What I've just read out to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: During the proofing, yes. However, prior to that, five years ago when it was drafted I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the Defence went over your NIOD interview with you in proofing?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you made comments on that to them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that there are a lot of inadequate translations. For example, I said that Zoran Petrovic-Pirocanac received 700 German marks, and here it says 700.000 German marks. You see, this is an example. During the operation, journalists were denied access, and it says here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, let's --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: -- that me and my assistants were denied access. So the translations are all inadequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 862, D862, page 19 in the English, page 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am surprised to see that with your feelings about NIOD you have actually cited NIOD as part of your report. But given that, let me read something that you say here and ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, but stop me, Mr. McCloskey, if it's a matter that you would touch upon anyhow. In what language was that interview conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that the -- your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had an English interpreter and the doctor was Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I just wanted to know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I can also perhaps clarify. The original of this document shown by Mr. McCloskey was in Dutch, and then the translations into B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is any concerns about Dutch-English, then I -- even I might cast an eye on it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question would be, do we have the Dutch original?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There are many, many thousands of pages. It is on the Internet. I don't suggest it would be a great idea to get into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: However, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- just this part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. This interview with the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you're speaking of the notes of the interview with the witness, that I do not believe is part of the report. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we always ask the witness to answer the question. The question is there is a Dutch version of this interview. Is that available, yes or no? The interview is we see English, we see B/C/S. Is this taken from a Dutch original and is that Dutch original available, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have a Dutch report in -- I don't know if it's an original or not. I don't know if they consider it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- Dutch or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, after the break I would like to hear from the Prosecution whether what is shown to us now, that seems to be the report on an interview, whether that's available in the Dutch language and whether the original is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it can be seen at 65 ter 31807.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm telling you this because -- yes, I see it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, but this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's all fine --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is a problem with the B/C/S channel, I'm told. The last several lines have not been coming through to Mr. Stojanovic or to Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know it's confusing but now we have the report of the interview on, before that we had the witness's statement on to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, what we have now is the -- apparently is the report on the conversation with Mr. Milutinovic on 20 and 22nd of March, 2000, and someone from the NIOD being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what I read to him in the English, the part about planned or operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps for others it's better not to stay with the Dutch, though Judge Moloto might understand some of it. But we are back in English now, and I -- if it is -- please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to say, if we look at that paragraph we can see whether it's 700 or 7.000, even if we don't know Dutch. At least that we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And -- yes, it's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let's -- we have paragraph 85 now on our screen which is about the number of written pages, which is not the same as the amount that was supposed to be paid to Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think it was paragraph 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was paragraph 53, if we could go back to the Dutch original. And I think that we can all see that it says 700.000. So if -- when we can go back to the witness's ICTY statement, D862, page 19 in the English, page 18 in the B/C/S. And I'm looking at paragraph 85, if we could blow that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where you say in your report, I won't read it all, but we do say that you talk about the Netherlands Institute for War Documentation which established after five years of research and 7.000 written pages that there were no plans whatsoever to commit crimes against the Muslim population in Srebrenica by either the civilian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not quoting correctly, Mr. McCloskey. It says that "no evidence was found about" which is not the same as what you read. It says not that there were no plans whatsoever, it says that there was no evidence about plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I'm reading, Mr. President, says: "After five years of research and 7.000 written pages, that there were no plans whatsoever to commit crimes against the Muslim population in Srebrenica by either the civilian or the military authorities of Republika Srpska and the FRY."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then it continues that: "The NIOD report was published in August 2002 and it explicitly states that no evidence was found about planning and the commission of genocide." So there may be even some inconsistency within this one paragraph, whether it is a positive finding of there being no planning or the absence of any evidence that there was planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and you interrupted me as I was reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree that I was reading a few lines further down with more or less the same language. And I should not have interrupted you at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'll keep going where you left off. "Their report confirms that there were crimes around Srebrenica, but according to their research, those were individual crimes as a result of extremism of certain armed groups." Now I would like to go to part of this voluminous NIOD report, 65 ter 31809. It should be page 7 in the English, page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, just for my -- for myself, is there -- in the Dutch version is that also uploaded of the report? It's not uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't read the first two paragraphs, but we can see that they are -- it's talking about Srebrenica enclave and -- a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The second paragraph begins with: "There is absolutely no doubt that the mass murder was committed by Bosnian Serb military units." And then the -- I'll read most of the third paragraph. And I'll quote NIOD saying: "There can be little doubt that the mass executions were carefully planned and organised. The hypothesis that they were more or less spontaneous as things 'got out of hand' is untenable. This said, certain of the smaller-scale killings, such as those at Kravica, Konjevic Polje, Bratunac, and Baljkovica, may have fallen into this category. It has not yet been determined who gave the order for these mass executions and whether the decision to proceed in this manner was a political or a military one. The larger-scale executions certainly demanded a degree of prior planning and organisation. In a generally well-structured and disciplined army such as the VRS, this would have required the foreknowledge and co-operation of the commanders. Transport had to be arranged for both prisoners and firing squads, bulldozers had to be deployed to - literally - cover up the consequences. It may still be possible to contend that the first executions were carried out by special units on the orders of the General Staff and by units of the Ministry of Home Affairs. However, it is clear that regular VRS units became embroiled in the crimes, supplying both personnel and equipment. These units would also have been involved in seeking locations for temporary detention of the men and suitable locations for executions, these locations being found at ever greater distances from Srebrenica. "It seems improbable that the mass murder was planned well in advance, although some Bosnians believe otherwise." So, sir, if we go back to your statement to the ICTY, and I quote page -- at your paragraph 85: "The NIOD report was published on 10 August 2002 and it explicitly states that no evidence was found about planning and the commission of genocide against the population in Srebrenica," as well as the rest of your paragraph which suggests. So how can you make this conclusion, sir? You obviously didn't read the NIOD report, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: When you were reading you yourself said that everything started from probabilities, that they didn't establish anything. NIOD says that there is no proof that executions had been planned. Second of all, a summary of this was published by IFP, and I just conveyed that. In my statement I never quoted that. I just gave an account of what was reported by the IFP agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So like you blame the last agency, you're saying it's the IP agency that made this conclusion about no planning and that's how this got into your report?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about that one agency. The first report was based on Tanjug, and this information was based on the AFP report as the first agency that ever published that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So as part of your report, you're really not getting into the primary source materials to determine reality from fiction, are you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "fabrication"? I did not fabricate anything. I just relied on a summary of the AFP News. Second of all, I used NIOD's information that the Tribunal had received my information which was shared in a free-flowing conversation that was held in Banja Luka 14 years ago. It was a long time ago, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're moving away from what the question is about. What Mr. McCloskey puts to you is that in your statement you do not say: "I read an excerpt or a summary of a report of NIOD prepared by agency so-and-so and they report that this is the case," but you -- in your statement you say the report says this, whereas I understand you have not read the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. 7.000 pages. I don't read Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have an opportunity to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming you for not having read it. What I'm saying to you is that your statement is inaccurate in this respect because it suggests that you read it and that you reflect what is in the report, whereas what you actually did is to read a summary. Now could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's inaccurate. I hope that we would agree on that. Then second, if you say it is the summary which was produced, do you still have a copy of the source you did consult and you did rely on when giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have time to bring this. If I'd known that it would be necessary. I was hoping that all the reports are here and that there was no need for me to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, all the original material is here. But the press clippings or the press messages you rely upon may not be here. So if at any stage you would still have it or still remember it or have it somewhere on your computer or whatever, then perhaps you could give it to the Tribunal so that we know -- although, we are more interested in primary sources than in what the press writes about a report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, why are you citing NIOD for authority when you're actually referring to some AP Press article? What kind of work product is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can have some clarification. Mr. McCloskey has gone from IFP, AFP, now to AP. As I understand it, those could be three different agencies. I'm no longer certain of what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- what's actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what press agency it exactly is not the core of the problem. Mr. McCloskey asked you why you are citing NIOD for authority where you're actually referring to some press article, some press summary, and what kind of a work product that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that I received NIOD - I didn't have to but I did - and our conversation lasted for ten years. And this summary after ten years of doing research on all the sides, Muslim, Croat, and Serb, was instrumental in using that and in stating what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not really --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- continue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- an answer to the question. But please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Going back to your statement D862, paragraph 17, you say that, and you're talking about events in 1992 and later, completely ignored were the extraordinary efforts on the part of the Portuguese Minister of Foreign Affairs, Jose Cutileiro, who brokered an agreement among all three sides, regarding the basis for organising the state into cantons which was signed by Alija Izetbegovic, Radovan Karadzic, and Mate Boban. Sir, I want to take to the 11th Session of the RS Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which is at P4580.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This occurred on 18 March 1992. And it's President Karadzic speaking of the Cutileiro document. And I quote: "The document has been accepted as a basis as a" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, e-court page 6, English page 7. If we want to get it up. English e-court, 6; B/C/S, 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'll quote. "The document has been accepted as a basis as a foundation for further negotiations. The document has not been signed. We would never sign anything that we did not agree upon." He goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: E-court page 43 in English, page 62 in the B/C/S, but it's short, and I will read it accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Karadzic: "I will have to provide at least a digested response to what has been said so far. What we have here is a process and the mistake that Dobrivoje Vidic is making has to do with the fact that an unfinished process should not be assessed as if it were a finished one. We have entered into this process with our strategic goals and we are accomplishing them stage by stage. "We would never have signed this paper as a document. Never, never, never!" You would agree with me that Radovan Karadzic knows better than you, as expressed in the assembly sessions, whether or not the RS signed the Cutileiro document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the information that I had, the document was initialed in Lisbon about the establishment of Bosnia and Herzegovina on a cantonal basis. Some agreements were reached and then the final signing agreements were supposed to be reached. If you're talking about the assembly session in March, at that time I was not in Republika Srpska at all so I was using archival materials in order to formulate the position. A couple of months ago Cutileiro visited Belgrade and he publicly stated that the document was initialed and that a high level of agreement was reached, and he was sorry that the American administration interfered. And this is on Radio Television Serbia. You can see Cutileiro's statement, who regretted that certain circles did not accept the basic points of the Lisbon plan because had that happened, there would have been no war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I take it when you were out of the RS you were not in Lisbon at the Lisbon Conference?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: There are documents, archives. Any researcher who wanted to study something could have access to different documents in order to get proper data from which he would be able to draw the appropriate conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel, you've told us about the data you've been relying on. My question was whether you were at the Lisbon Conference.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this is a little inadequate, this question. I wasn't at the Lisbon Conference and I was not at this assembly session in Pale, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, whether the question is inadequate or not is not for a witness to comment upon. You've given --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The president said at the 49th Session of the RS Assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 02410. It should be on e-court page 116 in English, page 79 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again, what President Karadzic says, and I quote: "The first position in all Cutileiro's principles, if you remember, was that Bosnia was a state consisting of this and that but it always said that Bosnia was a state, and we never accepted that and we demanded the maximum that we could accept. Bosnia is a confederation of states." You know the reality, don't you, that the RS government was never going to agree to a state shared with the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking for my position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska would have accepted and does accept -- or Bosnia-Herzegovina and did so until the point in time when the Sarajevo leadership demanded that Republika Srpska be abolished because that was allegedly a genocidal creation. If the attitude towards Republika Srpska had changed, and judging by the most recently elected government, the position is that Republika Srpska is a legitimate entity and Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P3106.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- and, Mr. McCloskey, what is the position or is not, the primary concern at this moment seems to be the reliability of the statement of the witness. Would you agree with me that where you state that the Cutileiro Plan was signed by Izetbegovic, Karadzic, and Mate Boban, that a more adequate description of the situation would have been that it was initialed and that in the follow-up conversations in parliamentary sessions that there was quite some dispute about how acceptable or not acceptable that was and -- as expressed by Mr. Karadzic? Because that's apparently what Mr. McCloskey puts to you, that this does not adequately reflect the situation. Would you, on the basis of what he has just shown you, would you agree or would you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that it was only initialed. That's what I said. The agreement was not signed as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what your statement says. Your statement says that it was signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I meant by that. That it was initialed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your statement also does not refer to any discussions in parliament in which the adherence to or the denial to accept the conditions of the Cutileiro Plan were discussed. And Mr. McCloskey puts it to you that that then, therefore, inadequately reflects the situation as it existed at the time. Do you agree that parts are missing, or do you say no, it still is an adequate reflection of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, you are completely correct. I was just using parts of it. And in the beginning I did say that because of the voluminous material the attorneys asked me to cut my statement short, and that's the reason why I did not go into all the elements in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not about -- only about details, it is also about whether the selection you made still reflects the main gist of the material that does exist. But let's leave it to that. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would offer that section of the 49th Assembly, 65 ter 02410, e-court page 116 in the English, 79 in the B/C/S, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the whole of the document been uploaded and can we deal with a selection rather than to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was hoping that was just one page, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm just seeking verification of it being an excerpt or it being the whole of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll make sure we get an excerpt in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- that just has that part, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's already reserve a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 02410 receives P7023, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did uploaded as an excerpt will be admitted. There are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Ms. Stewart informs me that should be 2410A as an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And these are the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has it been uploaded already or it's still to be uploaded? Then the number is reserved for what will be uploaded as 02410A. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to your ICTY statement, D862.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 21 in the English, page 20 to 21 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where you note that, in talking about Zepa: "I was present at the talks General Mladic had with the Muslim representatives of Zepa and the commander of the Ukrainian Battalion of UNPROFOR. The talks were also attended by General Zdravko Tolimir, the VRS Main Staff assistant commander for intelligence and security. Upon request of the Muslim side, it was agreed to organise the departure and transport from Zepa for the entire population and members of the brigade in Zepa. They were guaranteed transportation towards the federation of BiH and full safety." So in your view, the Zepa population willingly requested transport out of Zepa on their own free will?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it your position from that paragraph that the Muslim population of Zepa requested under their own free will to be transported out of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: We received that information from the commander of the Ukrainian Battalion who was stationed in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were with General Tolimir, did General Tolimir tell you that he had threatened the Muslim population that if they didn't evacuate military force would be employed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir never told me that. I was in the information service, so he was not duty-bound to inform me about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I intervene here. Witness, my problem is that you make statements in your statement as facts, and then when you are asked questions you tell us you were told this, you got this from another source. Now you say you were told by the - what is it? - the Ukrainian Battalion about what happened, that these people voluntarily left. But you are not saying that in your statement that you were told this by that battalion. You are just telling us this as a fact. This is the same -- this is the fourth time now we get an incident where you state things and then when you are asked you say: No, no, no I didn't read that, I got it from another source.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I attended the conversation between General Mladic and the Bosnia-Herzegovina UNPROFOR commander. At that time it was noted - there was a representative of the Ukrainian Battalion there, too - and he said that the Muslim side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the Ukrainian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not answering my question. My question is: Why do you tell us things as facts which you actually do not know? Which -- and you don't tell us that you were told this. You are talking in your statement as if you are talking as a first-hand person with first-hand knowledge, but when you are asked you tell us: No, no, no, I was told this by somebody or I read it in IPF, not in NIOD. This has been constant in your evidence this morning. Now, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I attended the meeting when the commander of the Ukrainian Battalion in charge of Zepa presented the position to General Smith and General Mladic. I was there and I heard it myself. This is not second-hand or third-hand information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. It is second-hand information to you, and that's exactly my question: Why in your statement don't you say: The Ukrainian Battalion told us this at the meeting? You're not -- there is no mention of the battalion in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. That's the point I'm making to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me show you P01471. This is a report on the 13th of July from General Tolimir to the Main Staff, sector for intelligence and security, and General Krstic personally, and others. Reporting on his contact with Hamdija Torlak and Mujo Omanovic who were the civilian representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we go to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, do we have the right number? Because the document on the screen is not what's being described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think now we have a document which comes closer to the description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we've got the right one up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, the translation seems to be an excerpt of the original? Because it starts with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and left out the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The part I want to show to him is the part right after the numbers. If we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we would like to know what we are looking at, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if in one way or another you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could blow the Serbian up, it's the complete document, I think. But it's just disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you can see it in page 1 of the English if you want them to match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There we have it. Now we know what we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 in the English, but for the Serbian, blow up the part just below number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as General Tolimir is talking about his contact with these Muslim representatives, he tells his superiors: "We rejected their first request and we made a condition that all necessary consultations had to be completed by 1500 hours and that the evacuation had to start at that time. We have conditioned this with an alternative solution - military force." So, sir, this is a real document, a serious report. And when civilian representatives are given the option either evacuate or face military force, the civilians really don't have any free will after that, do they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't know anything about this document. I'm seeing it for the first time. General Tolimir was not obliged to inform me about it. I was summoned by General Mladic simply to come to Zepa with a team of journalists. I arrived there and spent two or three days there while the evacuation of the people from Zepa was being prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So if this is an accurate report and the Muslims were facing this illegal threat or this threat, I won't say whether it's illegal or not, I take it you would like to withdraw paragraph 97 where you conclude that the Muslims left or -- where the Muslims were -- agreed to leave voluntarily or words to that effect? You would like to change that or delete it, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: My information, starting from the initial information, that that was what they opted for, I don't see -- I mean, the circumstances might have been different but the information that I had at that time, and even later, indicated that the Bosniaks requested to leave Zepa through the UNPROFOR command. But it's up to the Court to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: -- take that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You, yourself, did you get personally involved in communicating, helping the VRS to communicate to the civilians and other people in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I personally, with my journalists and even other journalists who were not part of the press centre, went down to Zepa. I was in Zepa practically that whole day during the preparations for the evacuation. I must say that I was wearing a uniform at the time, that I was in touch with many people who were there. And at any point in time did I feel anything of ill will from anyone of the people there among the population? It was quite the opposite. I was in the first buses to reach Boksanica, General Mladic was there, a CNN team was already there, and then General Mladic came into one of the buses, he shook hands and greeted everybody. There is footage of that. And General Mladic told everyone in each of those buses that they should not be afraid of anything, that they would all be transported to the territory of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and this is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did General Mladic mean when he said on videotape: "I see that there are able-bodied men among you. I give you your life as a gift"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't know what General Mladic meant. But the previous promise was that all those who laid down their arms could leave freely, so I wouldn't comment on that part of the statement because I really don't know what General Mladic meant when he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you know that Muslims, who you say were not afraid, had received information the Muslims from Zepa, that there had been mass killings in Srebrenica? You should -- certainly you would have heard about that by then, and did you know that the Muslim knew that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, even though I was chief of the information services of the army, up until that moment - which is 15 days later - practically did not know about the crimes that had occurred in Srebrenica. So if I was not aware of that, I don't know whether and through which channels the Bosniaks in Zepa could have been informed about it. All I'm saying to you is that I spent the entire day in Zepa, it was very cordial. I even had photographs taken with different people. Nothing unpleasant happened to me. Quite the opposite. I felt as if I were among normal people with whom you can establish communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you actually arrange with a security officer in Zepa that loudspeakers be used to give information to the Muslim population of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: There was that, yes. So that they do not put up resistance and for them to assemble in specific areas where they would be received by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, with messages like "resistance is futile"? You took part in that, personally?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, it is correct. I didn't take part in that personally, others did. But I was present when such messages were broadcast. And I think that this was very positive, because we did not have any problems in Zepa with the assembly of people, the departure, or any type of provocations during that entire procedure in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we see P3472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When we're waiting for it, Witness, you said "15 days later." Fifteen days later to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
