utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the people had been boarded in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you -- is it your evidence that 15 days after the departure of many inhabitants of Srebrenica that had boarded buses, that there was no knowledge whatsoever about large numbers of Srebrenica inhabitants or -- had lost their lives? Fifteen days later you would say nothing was known about that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, once people boarded the buses in Srebrenica, I went to my headquarters in Han Pijesak. I understand your question. I really, before Zepa, did not know what had happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not aware 15 days after the events that a large number of, especially men, had lost their lives when --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only knew of combat operations that were ongoing. And then for several nights, with some ten or 15 men I provided security for our own headquarters from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I was specifically avoiding any reference to how they lost their lives. Were you aware 15 days after the Srebrenica -- where the -- the population of Srebrenica being escorted out or leaving in any other ways, that a large number of men, I'm thinking in terms of thousands, had lost their lives? You were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is it your position that this was generally unknown to the -- even though rumours in the media, it was just unknown to everyone and therefore the population of Zepa could not have known about it? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not my position. I am not saying that they were not informed by some other sources, but I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you -- and I'll just read to you what you said a minute ago. One second, please. If the parties could assist me where the witness explained. I have some difficulties in finding where he --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Temporary transcript page 50, lines 6 through 12 -- 6 through 14, Your Honours, is the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said that you were not aware of that, apparently referring to what had happened in Srebrenica: "I don't know whether and through which channels the Bosniaks in Zepa could have been informed about that." Whereas you're now telling us that there may have been other sources that allowed them to get acquainted with information about persons being killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to the information that we received at the meeting with Rupert Smith, some 1.000 Bosniaks who had been in Srebrenica crossed the terrain across Zepa and went in the direction of Gorazde. I suppose that those could have been the people who informed the people in Zepa about the situation in Srebrenica or at least some elements thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I may point out, temporary transcript page 52, lines 7 through 9, the witness actually said the exact same thing, that he does not know. And in the first instance it was he does not know whether they were informed. So there is no contradiction as Your Honours had indicated with your question. The witness has testified twice identically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether you do not know and whether you do not know how someone could possibly have received -- could have received that information is not exactly the same. But let's leave it to that. We'll take a break first, and we would like to see you back in 20 minutes, Witness. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. If we could -- the excerpt from 65 ter 02410 has now been uploaded into e-court under 65 ter 02410A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we had reserved a number for that. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: P07023? I give Ms. Stewart credit for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, we might deal briefly with translation replacements. In relation to P6966, is there a new translation uploaded that should replace the old one, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, it has been uploaded, Mr. President, under doc ID 0671-2054-A-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the newly uploaded translation of which the doc ID was just mentioned by Mr. Tieger may replace the existing English translation in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar is instructed to that replacement. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just -- a simple document before you. I just wanted to confirm with you that this is accurate. It shows that you were in some way working with Captain Guduras, a security officer from the 1st Krajina Corps in -- in the use of those loudspeakers for Zepa. Does this reflect your memory of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to your -- the NIOD -- interview that you had with NIOD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 31807. Page 10 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's a very, very short note or part of their report that I'll read to you. Something they obviously are reporting that you told them. "Mladic was very interested in the opinion of the West. Every morning Milutinovic's organisation compiled an analysis of reports in foreign newspapers, and Mladic read them." So first of all, is the first sentence correct, that Mladic was interested in the opinion of the West during these war years?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Every commander needs to be informed. Therefore, he has to be aware of the public opinion and the position of the public towards certain issues. I agree that this is very correct. I had some dozen women who monitored the media. During that time, most of the time we did not have electricity and we could not follow the media. However, we made sure that the media summaries from Croatia, Bosnia, and Serbia, as well as the foreign media, especially BBC, was available to us. We then analysed those reports and submitted a summary of such media reports to the Main Staff. So this is true. I suppose that General Mladic received such information on top of other things, and he was thus abreast of the positions of the West vis-à-vis certain developments in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you knew a journalist named Robert Block or you knew of a journalist named Robert Block?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 19242.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is this paper called "The Independent," which I -- this is the same paper you cited in your report, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were just answering questions of the President regarding the issue of sources of information, what people may have known, when they knew it. So let's take a look at this article. We see that as early on as July 14th that information in this article is being disseminated. I won't go through the details of it, but it talks about the deportation of thousands of terrified Muslims being deported from Srebrenica. It also says in paragraph 5 that: "Men of fighting age have been taken away by the Bosnian Serbs for what they said was 'screening.'" So you were in the Hotel Fontana on the 12th of July at the morning meeting that has been filmed, were you not, where there were Muslim representatives there, it was a morning meeting, you had -- Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic was at your left and Radislav Jankovic was on your right. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to the question. It's a narrative mixing and matching now a document and then it's a -- it's pointing attention to a document and then going to another topic. If there is a question about the document, the question should be stated. We should not have a -- the Prosecutor testifying and giving us arguments about something, especially arguments that contradict his own witnesses about what happened in Srebrenica. We had General Cornelius Nicolai who said that the UN for the people to be removed from Srebrenica because of the hygenic conditions in the area. And now Mr. McCloskey is citing to a newspaper article, which apparently he wants in evidence, he's not asking the witness questions about the article. He's reading the article and then he's going on to different topic. It's highly improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I was still waiting for his question. I considered this to be a kind of a refreshment of the witness's memory as to his presence during that meeting and that we would then hear questions about what he introduced earlier. And I think the witness in his statement stated that he attended the meeting, although, Mr. McCloskey, who he was sitting to next, et cetera, may be details which the witness would not have needed to remember that he was at the morning meeting at Hotel Fontana. Were you there, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And now I take it that you move to questions in relation to the -- to what you introduced earlier, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Precisely. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this Court has heard evidence that at that morning meeting Mladic announced that men would be screened to look for war criminals. Is that correct? Did Mladic say something along those lines at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Mladic said something along these lines: All the men for whom there is a suspicion that they had committed crimes over the Serbian people would be kept. As far as I know, a number of those were kept and then five days later they were handed over to the Red Cross. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so this report that comes out two days later that makes a reference to screening, that's similar to what you had heard Mladic actually say at the meeting? People screened for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But one thing gets forgotten: In Eastern Bosnia, i.e., Podrinje, about 3200 Serbian civilians had died from 1992 onwards at the hands of Naser Oric and his criminal organisation. The Serbian authorities already had lists of those who had committed crimes and we had in mind those people who had been known or who were on our records as those who had participated in the commission of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, also in your statement we now and then see a reference to what is forgotten. What is forgotten by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you say: But things get forgotten. If you think that we are forgetting something, is that what you mean? Or the media? Or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not mean you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if the press had forgotten something then -- the media had forgotten something, that's none of our concern.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The media ignored that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that as well. Now, that is not of relevance for us unless a specific leaving out of information would turn out to be relevant for our determinations. But there is no need to, in general -- to say in general terms what was forgotten in the media or by the people or by whomever. So please refrain from such general statements. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, this article is the kind of thing that you would have wanted your team to be able to collect and provide information to General Mladic in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Probably I would have informed him about that. But let me repeat: We were completely isolated there. There was no electricity. We had generators and we could listen to the BBC, we could read Washington Post there and some other media but not many. In other words, we did not have access to all the media. I don't know what you had in mind. Robert Block was in Bosnia and Herzegovina on several occasions. We know that he authored a text to refute the allegation that Serbs raped a lot of non-Serb women. I know that on the 28th of June, 1995, during the liberation of the anniversary [as interpreted] of the Serbian army, I asked General Mladic to give an interview, a rather long interview to Block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're moving pretty far away from what the question was. Mr. McCloskey, could you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yup.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I take it from that you trusted Robert Block enough to have Mladic give him an interview, but your team wasn't with you in Potocari. They were back in Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka, were they not? Were they --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object. It's a compound question. Again, he's mixing two questions together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please split it up, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your team wasn't with you? Weren't members of your team still back at Han Pijesak or Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And they would have access to the wire services, to newspapers like "The Independent"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: BBC, Deutsche Welle, or the Voice of America. That's all we had access to. We did not receive any printed media. No printed media reached us. Every now and then we received articles or clippings from various newspapers by fax, but those communication lines were very bad and sometimes you had to wait for over a half an hour for just one page to be transmitted by fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19242 receives Exhibit P7024, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to another Robert Block article, 65 ter 12892.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This article -- we can see it's dated up near the top that it's dated July 17th. He's reporting out of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have -- we have two B/C/S documents, apparently not the same, on our screen. Could we have -- yes. There we are, I think. No. Well, I'm quite certain it's -- it's both "Independent" but could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the correct English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I wonder whether the B/C/S is the translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The B/C/S has the date 14 July. This document has the date 23 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the B/C/S version next to the English one. There we are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this shows that he is reporting out of Belgrade. So you had -- you're especially -- your headquarters in Crna Rijeka or Han Pijesak had access to communications from Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: There was just one line, which was often down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, clearly you received information from official sources in Belgrade in your work for -- in public information?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that we did not have anybody in Belgrade. We were part of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have a single associate in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question was not whether or not you had someone in Belgrade but whether you received information from official sources in Belgrade. You don't need to have someone in Belgrade to receive that information. Did you receive information from official sources from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to Tanjug? Is that who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm referring to nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have communication with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you did have communication with Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Their correspondents came to see me in Han Pijesak. I must admit that during the war I received about 4700 foreign journalists and I had briefings with all of them, and that's how our positions were communicated. We issued communiques or we organised press conferences, and that's how we conveyed our message to the general public or received messages from the general public in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I won't go over all of this, but please take a look at it. It's describing a video that apparently Robert Block had seen. And he talks about seeing, in the third paragraph, the horror of Srebrenica, and he had the technician stop the film, and I quote: "When the technician stopped the film, there it was, in freeze-frame, the horror of Srebrenica, in piles two feet high. The bundles were clearly not empty clothes. They were heads, arms, and legs. The fit body of a young man in the foreground filled out a white T -shirt. The bodies up against the wall looked to be three deep in places. It was impossible to make out the exact number, but 25 would be a reasonable guess." He goes on to talk about stains and bullet holes. And then he mentions: "The implication of the report by the independent Serb television channel Studio B, which was not overtly pro-Bosnian Serb but clearly sympathetic, was that these were Muslim soldiers killed in combat. The scene, however, looked more like a place of summary execution than of combat." Now, are you aware of this famous footage referred to -- that was taken by a journalist that you have mentioned in your report named Zoran Petrovic, known as Pirocanac?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Pirocanac is not from Republika Srpska. He was not a member of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, please listen to the question. The question is whether you are aware of the footage which is referred to in this article by Mr. Block and which, as Mr. McCloskey suggests, is made by Mr. Petrovic, are you aware of that footage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I became aware of that footage only some 10 to 15 days after the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this article is a description of that footage, is it not? That footage shot by Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Are you waiting for my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a simple question. This -- this article is describing the Petrovic film, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: That Petrovic film shows that for only a few seconds. I didn't see anything special in that footage, save for that one second perhaps that was shown of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you would agree with me that this article detailing what I have read out is a description of that film? He mentions Studio B.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I agree that that may well be the case. However, if something is shown only for one second, I believe that that one second is not relevant. It doesn't have to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I only learned about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we are not discussing at this moment how relevant that this. Mr. McCloskey would like to know, and you have answered that question, that what is described here, that you think it's well possible that that's a description of the Petrovic video. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Block says that this tape was shot on the Thursday, two days after Srebrenica was overrun. The Court has heard evidence that that film was shot on the 13th of July, which I'm sure the Defence would agree was two days after the 11th when Srebrenica was taken. So we can see that the world has been made aware of the events depicted in this film just four days after they occurred on 17 July. You'd agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have information that it had reached that level. You know there was a war going on and situations like that always result in human loss. I didn't know how much of that was true, whether it was real. There were a lot of games being played in Bosnia and one had to wait for the information to be corroborated and verified in order to come out with the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milutinovic, will you please answer the question now. The question is would you agree with Mr. McCloskey that by the 17th of July the world was informed about what happened in Srebrenica four days earlier? Do you agree or don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But -- but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's enough. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this the kind of information that General Mladic would have wanted to know about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes. Certainly. And I believe that we managed to convey part of that information to the Main Staff. But we did not know whether those were individual or group or mass executions, and what kind of a crime had been committed in that area. What's the extent of the crime committed in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one short follow-up question. You also did not know who had committed those crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 12892 receives Exhibit Number P7025, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell us, if you will, any specific efforts you personally made to obtain a copy of the Petrovic film?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Some ten days later I learned about the existence of that film. Some journalists from Belgrade informed me about its existence, which means that I learnt there and then about that existence. Journalists informed me that they were ready to hand that film over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I informed the Main Staff, i.e. General Tolimir, that a film of that kind existed. I told him where it was and how to obtain it, because journalists were willing to hand it over to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly how long after Srebrenica fell did you inform General Tolimir of this film?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Some ten days later, after having received confirmation from the journalists who had arrived from Belgrade that a film of that kind existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So going back to our chronology of -- Srebrenica fell on the 11th of July, roughly ten days would be the 21st of July. Tolimir and you and General Mladic were together in Zepa. And the bus that Mladic got on as the Zepa folks were leaving was the 25th of July. So by the time General Mladic got on the bus and made his comments, he would have been aware of the existence of the Petrovic film.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: He may have known because I informed General Tolimir that there was a film, that it was in Belgrade, and that journalists were willing to hand it over. I don't have any subsequent information as to whether that was done or not, and if it was, who was it who had taken the film over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a question. As chief of the information centre, did you not inform General Mladic in -- as soon as you became aware of the existence of this film that there was such a film in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that I did not serve as directly subordinated to General Mladic but to Milan Gvero, the assistant commander for information, morale guidance, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I told him of the existence of the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You've testified earlier today that you and your assistants compiled information in the press centre which you passed on to Mr. Mladic. I'm just asking you whether you did not tell Mr. Mladic immediately you heard of the existence of the film that such a film did exist. Yes or no? You told Tolimir. Did you tell Mr. Mladic? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I drafted reports to the Main Staff, you know. Not to General Mladic personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If I can stop you there. I see you don't want to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then my information was distributed in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's leave it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You knew, didn't you, that General Mladic left the Bratunac area where you had been with him on the 13th and travelled right by -- right along that road where those bodies were piled up, the same day that they were -- it was filmed. You must have known that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could you first of all split up the matter. Whether it misstates the evidence, I think that in a leading question it's not necessarily what is already the evidence. But if there is any clear contradiction, Mr. McCloskey, it would be better to avoid that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the Prosecution has indicated and asked the witness to agree, and I think even asked the Defence to agree, that this is the Petrovic video which, my understanding is, shows Kravica which is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- a road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you're now aware of what apparently is on the mind of Mr. Ivetic. Could you please take matters step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then just to complete, Your Honours. The videotape of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to -- he's now arguing and he's trying to communicate something to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Without the witness I'll repeat the same things. This is an objection to the manner of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if there is anything that could possibly --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should remain silent. He knows what the consequences would be. If there is anything that could possibly be understood as a hint to the witness, you should ask the witness to take his earphones off first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I'll ask the witness to take his earphones off, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please take your earphones off, Witness. Mr. Mladic is supposed to sit down and he can consult with Mr. Stojanovic at a nonaudible - nonaudible - volume. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will simplify my objection in the most simple manner possible: Is it the Prosecution's position and what evidence they are citing in this question that General Mladic was present at Kravica on the afternoon when the footage was shot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is -- you are seeking the position of the Prosecution. Mr. McCloskey, you are suggesting to the witness that Mr. Mladic traveled a certain trajectory on a certain day. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, my --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because if that's the case, then it's running afoul of the joint submission we made with the Prosecution that they stipulated to as to the whereabouts of General Mladic. So that's why I'm asking. Because if we don't have an agreement, I'm going to ask for more evidence to be brought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, could you please, and forgive me for not having the stipulation exactly on my mind in this moment, in violation of what exact stipulation you think Mr. McCloskey is asking a leading question from the witness? Could you please answer my question, Mr. Ivetic. And I would prefer you listen to me rather than to talk to Mr. Stojanovic when I'm addressing you. But please, what exactly -- what stipulation exactly you say Mr. McCloskey is acting contrary to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have, the Prosecution and the Defence, about the whereabouts of General Mladic during the time-period of July the 13th through July the 16th have presented to the Chamber agreement as to facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At no point in time has it been suggested that General Mladic was in Kravica during the time-period that the Petrovic video was filmed and that the alleged scenes depicted in that video would have been -- would have been filmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the stipulation --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the stipulation exclude, leaves no room for the possibility that Mr. Mladic would have been on the date at which the footage was shot in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I submit, since the Prosecution has rested their case, that, yes, that since they have not presented evidence of that during their case in chief they are precluded from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, I'm also inviting you to listen to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say that the Prosecution is acting against the stipulation, and I asked you whether the stipulation is such that it excludes what Mr. McCloskey is suggesting to the witness. That's my question. Not whether they have presented evidence or not on matters. And could we just have the stipulation. I have the text here now. Yes. I have it before me. Does this stipulation exclude the presence of Mr. Mladic. And could we have another copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My recollection is the only part that was in dispute was when General Mladic returned to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- the theatre of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether it would have been on the 16th, the 17th, and what time. That was what was the communications between the parties at the time that the stipulation was being prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I again stress -- yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I am looking at the text of the stipulation and I'm asking myself, because that's the objection, whether Mr. McCloskey, by putting this question, is not honouring what he stipulated to. And I suggest that you have a close look at it. If you need a copy, we'll provide you with a copy, rather than to work on the basis of what you seem to remember. It may well be all true or not, but I just -- I would like to have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my objection was not based on the stipulation. My explanation was based on the stipulation. My objection was that it misstates the evidence. There has been no evidence led during the Prosecution's case in chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is it your position that in a leading question you can only put something to the witness which -- for which evidence has been received, or isn't it one of the specific features of a leading question that you can suggest to a witness a fact which has not yet been established? I thought always that's my understanding of what a leading question is, which is permitted in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When it relates to the alleged presence of the accused at a site where a crime is alleged to have happened, I believe the Prosecution has an obligation to lead that evidence in their case in chief and not to try to present questions as if it's been proven when it's not been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I might be able to help here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're switching -- you're switching --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's been my objection since the very first point. I stated it very succinctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now this video was taken on the 13th of July is your suggestion, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- doubt very much that's even contested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- think I can clear this up, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's look at the agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, he's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- Mr. McCloskey, give me one second. Give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just trying to help you, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The agreed facts are split up in dates, 13 July, 14 July, 15 July, 16th of July. The one and only fact agreed upon for the 13th of July is: On the evening of 13 July, General Ratko Mladic was at the Main Staff's command post in Crna Rijeka. Nothing in addition to that. So therefore whether it misstates the evidence is a different matter. I think that -- but it certainly does not, as was your argument earlier, violate in this respect what was agreed which is only where Mr. Mladic was at the evening of the 13th of July, that is, in Crna Rijeka. Let's leave it to that. Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could briefly respond, he's asked for our position. He's made some serious allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think I can help clear this up. He's misunderstood what I have said. I did not say that General Mladic was at the Kravica warehouse when the Petrovic film was being filmed. I said, which is clear in the question, that General Mladic went along the same road on the same day that Petrovic went. And I will make as a factual -- he asked for our position. Our position is that in the afternoon General Mladic went by the Kravica warehouse, stopped at the Sandici meadow, and gave a speech. This is -- he's agreeing with me. And after he left the Sandici meadow, within a period of time, it's not exactly clear, one to two to three hours, perhaps, men from the Sandici meadow were taken to the Kravica warehouse and butchered. Mladic went on after the Sandici meadow to Konjevic Polje, talked to people, then he went on to Nova Kasaba, and that's the facts that I'm speaking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think that it's clear to Mr. Ivetic. What I would suggest to you is that where you suggested Mr. Ivetic misunderstood your question, that we ask the witness to put his earphones on again, and that you in short, brief questions revisit the matter you intended to visit ten minutes ago. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that General Mladic had driven by the area where these bodies were filmed the same day they were filmed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: After boarding the buses and the recording, I went --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd ask you to answer my question. We're getting --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: -- to Han Pijesak and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's getting late. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where Mladic went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this in -- excuse me, it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell us what personally you did to try to obtain the Petrovic video? Did you -- well, strike that. Did you ever get the Petrovic video?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I informed the relevant people in the Main Staff that there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm stopping you there. The simple question is whether you ever obtained a copy of that video. Did you or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I have a follow-up question. You talked earlier of just one second of that video being shown. How do you know it was just one second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a question, did I receive it? I saw it but I did not receive a copy and I did not have it in the archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the VRS receive a copy of this video?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff did receive a copy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you're distinguishing between yourself and the Main Staff. Aren't you a member of the Main Staff, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have a copy of the film. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the more precise the questions are, the less you run into problems as you ran in a minute ago. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What involvement did you have in getting the Main Staff a copy of this video?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I just informed the authorised security services that there was footage. I gave the names of people in Belgrade who had the footage, and then I did not have anything more to do with this matter. It was not in my jurisdiction anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who from the security service are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who brought the tape back?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's look at P1482.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No need, I don't think, to go through all of this. But this is a document dated 22 June 1996 in your name. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And these are your efforts in communicating to the security branch to get this tape from these folks in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1484.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see that we now have this, a document, the authorised official of the VRS security body, dated 24 June. And it's a receipt for temporarily seized objects. And it's from the person that you had mentioned in your document, and the object was received by a Naval Captain Ljubisa Beara. So you would have known that Beara came back with a tape that was the subject of your communication?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: But only one year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you agree with me that you knew Beara went to Belgrade and got this tape and brought it back?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm saying that it was one year later, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We agree, as we said, that it was in June 1996. The question is simple. You wrote the document to the security branch to get the tape, and you know that Beara brought it back. Is that yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I was informed that it was handed over to the Main Staff, but I don't know then what happened to that footage later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 19246.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another article from Robert Block, this one dated July 21, 1995. It's entitled: "Mass slaughter in a Bosnian field knee-deep in blood." I don't want go over the details. We can see that it basically reports -- Block is reporting that there had been many people killed after Srebrenica. Was this the kind of information General Mladic would have wanted to be aware of that was out in the public?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Western public. It was published on the 21st of July. I could have received it only 15 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer my question? Would this have been the kind of information General Mladic would have wanted to know?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: He did receive some texts from our service. I don't know whether this particular text was passed on to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19246 receives Exhibit Number P7026, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last article from Robert Block, 65 ter 19244.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This one's dated July 25th, 1995, entitled: "'River killings' shed light on scale of horror after the fall of Srebrenica." And in this article he reports that people on the Serbian side of the Drina see killings and they go over and they take a man that is named in this article, Resid Halilovic, over to Loznica. Is Loznica across the river, more or less, from a place called Kozluk? Kozluk's in Bosnia, Loznica's in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you heard of this account but not under the name Resid Halilovic, under the name of Resid Sinanovic, who was a former police officer in the Srebrenica police department before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19244 receives Exhibit Number P2 -- 7027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7027 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 31714, but it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a -- this is an intercept conversation, sir, that is dated on the 13th of July, the -- from the CSB of Tuzla. And it basically says on the 13th of July, and I'll quote: "The same day at 2335 hours we recorded a conversation between journalist Goran Malnaga and Vesna Stupar." Who is Goran Malnaga?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We still don't have the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see an image of the document here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you verify the number, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be broadcast. Mr. McCloskey, the Registrar has some difficulties in getting anything else on the screen under that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm fine if we don't see it. It's pretty short and I'll be very careful. It's -- I'm sure we'll figure it out because it's -- we've confirmed these, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, for the time being you may proceed. But please be extremely accurate on what you quote from a document we have not on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Janet says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There we are. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I was reading that first paragraph and I ask you who Goran Malnaga was.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: A journalist at the press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Vesna Stupar?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: She covered Bosnia and Herzegovina Radio. She was an analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. From the press centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it goes on to say that -- it talks about the conversation between those two people and the chief of the Main Staff press centre, Lieutenant-Colonel Milovan Milutinovic, who they couldn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Main Staff press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Main Staff press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's you, obviously? And --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the -- the CSB folks conclude, they say, as you can see next: "We drew the following conclusion from the conversation: "The Main Staff issued an order that no information related to Srebrenica or Zepa must be made public until further notice." So having in mind what the Muslims say they overheard these two people talking to you about, I would like to go to P02120.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could find where the document says that this was discussed. It says this is the conclusion reached by the individuals who are allegedly listening to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They say it's a conversation between the three people. They couldn't hear Mr. Milutinovic. That's all I meant by "discussed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So basically what you're going to see is an order dated the same day as this intercept from General Mladic that everyone will agree, I think, has to do with preventing information leakage. And I know this was a long time ago, Colonel, but do you recall on that period around 13 July receiving an order or reading this order or an order like it from General Mladic and then talking to Goran and Vesna about it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that it was a long time ago. I personally don't remember this document. And the two people that you referred to, I don't think that they -- they are just regular members of the press centre. And in any event, perhaps they could have been talking about this, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So perhaps they could have been talking with you about this topic. That would have been normal under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible. But I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm looking at the clock. We should take a break. Could you tell us how much more time you would need after the break? Because we are close to the two hours you claimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll keep it to the two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let me just ask Madam Registrar to give us detailed information so that you know how many more minutes you have. Mr. Ivetic, as matters stand now, could you give us an indication as how much time you would need in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ten minutes or under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes or under. You have ten minutes left, Mr. McCloskey. The Chamber may have a few questions as well. Witness, we take a break of 20 minutes. We would like to see you back after that. And we resume at a quarter to 2.00. Ten minutes remaining, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I would like to briefly deal with the following matter; that is, the Defence motion to admit the evidence of Witness Milan Tutoric pursuant to 92 ter. On the 19th of November, the Defence filed a motion, a 92 ter motion, for Milan Tutoric. On the 3rd of December, the Prosecution filed its response objecting to the admission of evidence on the grounds that, inter alia, the written statement, first, contains inadmissible opinion evidence and, two, lacks relevance and fails to meet the minimum threshold of reliability. The Prosecution further objects to the introduction of an expert opinion from this witness who is presented by the Defence as a witness of fact. The Chamber would like to hear by Monday, the 12th of January, 2015, an additional submission from the Defence as to whether this witness would be more appropriately presented as a expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I'd had a number of housekeeping matters that I've refrained from raising because of time considerations. There is one, however, that may have some time-sensitive implications. So if the Court has any time at the end of the day for one minute to go into private session to address it, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll certainly -- we're getting nervous as well, Mr. Tieger. Mr. McCloskey, your last ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to take you briefly back to that morning meeting at the Hotel Fontana where you were there with the Muslim representatives and General Mladic made the comment about the screening for war criminals or something to that effect. And that was being filmed, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic asked me to come with a journalist and a cameraman, and we recorded that conversation by VHS cameras. Having provided the necessary information, General Mladic insisted that we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the simple answer is: Yes, it was filmed. Please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1148, which should be e-court page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This, for simplicity's sake, is a still of a -- of a film clip that we received many years ago of that meeting. And I'd just want to ask you a question or two about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think if we could blow it up. I don't think we need the -- what's on the left side, and I don't think the identifications is really an issue. So I say we don't need the part on the left. I don't -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you see yourself in this photo?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I do. In the back of the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that number 3?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Number 3, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this, as you remember it, basically the scene that -- at the Hotel Fontana about the time that Mladic made these -- these words about screening for possible war criminals?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: That photo was taken after General Mladic had his conversation with Karremans, and Mladic had agreed to meet with the Muslim delegation the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But my --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Many of these people I saw for the first time, because I'd not had any need to communicate with them ever before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Mladic's statements to Karremans about screening the prisoners was filmed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you were able to sell that film?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at 65 ter 20925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm somewhat puzzled by you calling this the morning meeting and the witness saying that they agreed that the next morning, I think, they would meet with -- the following day. Now, I may be mistaken, but is there any inconsistency there, "the following day"? You are talking about the morning. But was there a morning meeting with another meeting the following day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am aware of various meetings. I'm not aware of any meeting with this entire group the following day, so that is something that -- that you have identified as a possible complication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, would you please keep in mind that you were talking about a morning meeting and the witness said something about this picture where the next day they would meet again and whether that would be -- I just leave it to you, but -- you said -- let me see. The witness said, at page 85, that the photo was taken after General Mladic has had this conversation and had agreed to meet with the Muslim delegation the following day, which suggests that it's the day before the meeting with the -- and you said paragraph, page 83, line 25, to take the witness briefly back to that morning meeting at the Hotel Fontana. If that causes you no concerns, then I stay out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we -- the important thing is the morning meeting at the Hotel Fontana with this group where General Mladic made the comment about the screening of war criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This photo represents that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe before you do so, Mr. McCloskey, you can just check whether the 65 ter number you called is correctly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should not be played. And it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, but the number. The number on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and it's apparently not. It should be 20925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you then resume where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. We could go back to the other -- the still photo, the -- that was e-court page 66, P1148.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, we're just going to go back to try to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking at audible volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the question was: Was this the morning at the Hotel Fontana where Mladic made the comment to the assembled group around this table about screening the war criminals?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the photo was taken in the evening after the conversation with Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I can tell you that this is a still of a video that was shot on the 12th of July in the morning when General Mladic was with this entire group. I can show you another photo. Maybe it will help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 1148, e-court P -- page 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This should be the people that are sitting on the other side of you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the following day. Karremans and a Muslim delegation from Srebrenica, when Mladic presented his positions to him, i.e., that all those who surrendered their weapons could decide whether to go to Serbia, to the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the previous day -- could we look at the other picture again. I take it that by careful analysis of the video pictures and the -- such as things on the table, et cetera, that there should be a possibility to verify whether it's same day or the other -- or another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, there is no -- there will be no dispute on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed. I don't know how important it is but I noticed that there seemed to be a different understanding of what exactly it was that was depicted here. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So on that morning of -- the morning that you meet with all these people that we just saw in the two pictures, did Mladic make the statement that morning that war criminals would be screened, something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, General Mladic said that to the Muslim delegation. He told them that everybody could come freely, lay down their weapons, and that then they could go wherever they wanted to go without any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I am asking you about the comment about screening for war criminals. Did he make that comment that morning at this meeting that we see the two pictures of?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that happened at this particular meeting or the meeting with the Muslim delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sir, maybe I can help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the other photograph, which is the -- it's another still from the same video. It's page 64. It's just the other side of the table where the Muslims are sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the same video, it's the same hotel, it's the same people. Is this the delegation that Mladic made the statement about war criminals to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you've stated, this was filmed and you sold the film. Who did you sell the film to of this meeting of the Muslim delegation?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic said that the video recordings from Srebrenica should be made public, to show the public that we had nothing to hide, that we had done everything as we should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no one asked you who made you sell that film, why you sold that film. The question is to whom did you sell that film.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Repeat? I think it was Reuters. Do you need an explanation at all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We just need an answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one last exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we missed the answer of the witness, though, because he said some acronym and then he started talking and then we only heard "Reuters." There was a lot more there that was missed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Without giving an explanation could you just repeat your answer, which included a reference to Reuters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we sold this to Reuters and that they brought some 5.000 dollars and that that was paid into the Main Staff's fund.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see one last exhibit, 65 ter 20925. This, out of an abundance of caution, should not be broadcast. It's an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is another CSB intercept. This one's dated 12 July and there is actually a summary of two intercepts, one at 1435 hours and one at 1520 hours. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm going to interrupt you. The 65 ter number you give is exactly the same as the 65 ter number of the previous document. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We had the right one up there, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see in the first conversation they've got -- they are mentioning some people, Vesna Stupar again, ITN, and some others, and you. And it sounds like it's talking about the video and selling it. It's the second one I wanted to ask you about. We see that the intercept people are right down at -- near the bottom, it said: "He said that it is about five hours of uncut material and that he offered 15 minutes of it to the agency that Vojo represents for the prices of 30.000 DM. In the conversation that went on for a long time, Milutinovic managed to agree on the sale of the material for 25.000 DM." Is that correct, did you sell that for about 25.000 DM?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, because no agency was interested in it at more than 5.000 dollars. And we spoke to ITN, IFP, and Reuters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you sold edited material, you didn't sell them the whole five hours?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: No. They were interested in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you -- just lastly, I can tell you that the investigation in this case has never found a video of the Hotel Fontana meeting that you talk about as the one with the Muslim representatives, where the -- Mladic's statement about screening war criminals was present. Who edited the film that was sold?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: We had a journalist and we had a cameraman who had recorded that. They edited the thing to show the events in Srebrenica within five minutes, and then the complete material was handed over to the archives of the Main Staff. I later learned, when Biljana Plavsic brought IFOR to the command of the Main Staff, that that part of the video archives was part of the documentation that SFOR brought with them, as part of some 150 kilogrammes of various materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Lastly, in any event you'll agree with me that the VRS edited out the part of the video where Mladic talks about screening war criminals?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: If that was done, it was done unintentionally. I didn't have any reason to cut it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you later learned that all those people that were separated in Potocari were summarily executed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If we can have Exhibit P1482 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the -- one of the documents that Mr. McCloskey just presented to you. And in reference to the date, I think when it comes up you'll see it's June 1996. There we see now it's the date June 22nd, 1996, and you kept telling Mr. McCloskey only one year later, one year later. I want to ask you to clear up for us: Did the Main Staff obtain a copy of the Pirocanac video in 1996 or at the time of the Zepa operation which was June -- or, pardon me, July of 1995? If you know.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: There were rumours about that video-clip and its existence. However, we learnt about its existence and whereabouts only in 1996. As the chief of that service, I reacted immediately and said that we needed to get that video recording as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've had evidence at this trial from the Prosecution's own investigator Mr. Blaszczyk, at transcript page 11527 to 11528, that the raw footage in the possession of the Mr. Petrovic-Pirocanac was missing this segment relating to Kravica. Do you know if the tape that the Main Staff received in 1996, did it have this couple seconds' footage from Kravica or was it a copy that did not have that stuff from Kravica? Again, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now I would like to focus on your discussions with NIOD. You mentioned during cross-examination that you were relying upon a summary of the NIOD report -- pardon me, the NIOD report I would like to focus on. You said you were relying upon a summary of the NIOD report, and you are quoted as saying IFP which was later AFP and which later became AP. Could you clarify for us what agency had authored the summary of the NIOD report upon which you were relying when discussing the findings?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was IFP.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And whose agency is that? What country do they operate out of?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's a French agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I would like to focus on the NIOD discussions with yourself. You told us that the discussions with yourself were in Serbian and that there was an English translator present. To your knowledge, was there a Dutch translator present or were all the discussions in English and in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - and it was a long time ago, 14 years ago - everything was in Dutch or English --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: In Serbian or English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in terms of those discussions with you, did you ever have an opportunity to review any notes or summary of that meeting in any language subsequent to -- at the time that you had the discussions with the representatives from NIOD?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: The introduction and the conversation with NIOD lasted for three days, for ten hours all together. They promised that when everything was over that they would send me a summary to approve. After that I never saw this report until the moment I was proofed for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, again, on behalf of General Mladic and the rest of my team, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was under ten minutes. I hope that that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly helps. I'm afraid that I'm disturbing now the order a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, your interviews with the NIOD, were they recorded in any way, I mean by audio? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was just the hand-held -- it was a long time ago, 14 years ago, and they did record it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was recorded. Now, I do not know, I'm addressing the parties, that where there seems to be some dispute about whether it accurately reflects what the witness said, it may assist the Chamber if the parties could perhaps agree on receiving audio and verifying what is more plausible, that there was a distortion of what the witness said or whether it reflects what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of an audio. I would have to defer to the Prosecution, though, since -- well, we didn't have the entirety of the -- we didn't have all the languages of the interview until a day or so ago, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see that. But you introduced this material into evidence. But I take it that the Prosecution will certainly assist in trying to seek ways of verifying the accuracy of the interview and the summary of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that -- I believe we -- I'll check and see if we have an audio. This, as you might imagine, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you have it or whether you can obtain it, but there seems to be dispute about the matter and the Chamber always prefers to have disputes to be resolved rather than to -- remaining hanging above us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, just so you know, this is very sensitive material for the Dutch Institute. They rely on confidentiality many times to carry these things out, and we'll look into the possibility of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the parties would look at it on a confidential basis and agree on whether it reflects or does not reflect what the witness told during his interview. But I'm just encouraging you to explore ways by giving an opportunity to the Chamber to better assess the probative value of the evidence of this witness against the background of any possible recording of the interview he gave. Nothing more and nothing less at this moment. Witness, I've a few questions for you. In paragraph 16 of your statement, you say that the Vatican pressured the recognition of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you tell me exactly what your sources are for this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: In early 1992, in Belgrade but also in the republics, an emissary of the Pope visited and after the talks he immediately accused the Serbian side - there are documents, they can be found in the archives in Belgrade and elsewhere - where he, in an argumented manner, tried to accused the Serbs for all the events. What I would particularly like to note is that Pope Wojtyla, on the 8th of March, 1993, at St. Paul's Square, instead of calling for peace he begged God to punish the Serbs with bombing. And there are written records of this, written documents. So with this in mind I said that the Vatican throughout the entire war in its way tried to place itself on the side of one side only and protect it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Just for me to understand, are you saying that on the 8th of March, 1993, the Pope begged God to punish the Serbs with bombing? Is that -- is there any recording of that? I would -- Mr. Mladic should refrain from any expressions when the witness is giving his testimony. I -- it could well be that the Pope was at St. Paul's Square. I take it that that is easy to be verified. But what he said in March 1993 cannot explain the pressure by the Vatican in April 1992. Could you be a bit more precise on who visited, who was it, the representative of the Pope? You remember who it was?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who it was now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And did he accused the Serbs of something or did he say you -- the republic of -- one second, please. Or did he say that the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina had to be recognised?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: He did not mention Bosnia and Herzegovina at all. He accused the Serbs for the events in Croatia and for the beginning of the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's understood what the source is and what the source exactly contained. I have another question for you. You say that Fikret Alic, and that's paragraph 44 of your statement, was suffering from tuberculosis. What's your source for that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Trnopolje is my birthplace. I knew most of the people there. And after that footage, the locals there said: Why did they take him? Because he's suffering from tuberculosis. So it comes from the place itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where you say in paragraph 44: "Fikret Alic was suffering from tuberculosis." What you intended to say was Fikret Alic was said to suffer from tuberculosis by other persons living in Trnopolje. Did you ever see any medical record of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If the parties would have any additional information, of course the Chamber is always willing to address that. Finally, I have a question on paragraph 109 where you discuss the -- what happened on the Markale market in Sarajevo on the 5th of February, 1994, usually referred to as Markale 1 in this courtroom. You say the French television quoted a UN report on the explosion and you said what a certain journalist, Mr. Walker, said about that; namely, that the UNPROFOR report would have stated that the bomb was fired from the Muslim positions. If there is any UNPROFOR report which clearly states that, would you know -- have you seen that report?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN MILUTINOVIC
